fields.meta_title: How to Wait on God (When the Answer Is Slow)
fields.description: Waiting on God is not idle passivity but confident, expectant trust. Here is what it means to wait on God, why he makes us wait, and how to wait well.
fields.body_html:
Waiting is one of the hardest things God ever asks of us. We live in a hurried age that treats every delay as an enemy, and when our prayers are not quickly answered, when guidance is slow to come, when a longed-for change tarries year after year, we grow anxious, restless, and tempted to force matters ourselves. Yet Scripture speaks again and again of waiting on God as one of the great secrets of a strong and fruitful life. Far from being wasted time, waiting is where God does some of his deepest work in us. “They who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). Here is what it means to wait on God, and how to do it well.

What waiting on God really means

Waiting on God is not passive idleness, as though we simply sat with folded hands doing nothing. It is an active posture of the heart — a confident, expectant leaning on God, trusting him to act in his time and way. The word carries the idea of a servant attending on a master, alert and ready, and of hope stretching forward with quiet confidence. “I wait for the Lord, my soul waits, and in his word I hope” (Psalm 130:5).

So to wait on God is to keep trusting when we cannot yet see, to keep praying when the answer delays, to keep obeying while the outcome is hidden. It is the opposite of both panic and passivity. It refuses to run ahead of God in anxious self-effort, and it refuses to give up in despair. It simply holds its position, watching for God like a sentry watching for the dawn: “my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning” (Psalm 130:6).

Why God makes us wait

If God loves us and is able to act at once, why does he so often make us wait? Scripture gives several reasons, and understanding them turns waiting from a frustration into a work of grace. First, waiting deepens our trust, teaching us to rely on God himself rather than on his gifts or our own timetables. Second, it prepares us for what he is about to give; the delay is often God getting us ready for the answer. Third, his timing is simply wiser than ours: “For still the vision awaits its appointed time... If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come” (Habakkuk 2:3).

There is even a beautiful reversal in Scripture: while we wait for God, God is waiting for the right moment to bless us. “Therefore the Lord waits to be gracious to you... blessed are all those who wait for him” (Isaiah 30:18). The delay is not divine neglect but divine wisdom, timing the gift for the moment it will do us the most good. God is never late, though he is often slower than we would like — and his slowness is a form of his love. A fruit ripened too quickly is sour; a bond stretched and held through a long wait is stronger than one never tested. What looks from our side like delay is, from his, the careful timing of a Father who is never careless and never in a hurry, and who withholds nothing good from those who walk before him.

Wait with quiet trust, not anxious striving

The great temptation in waiting is to take matters into our own hands — to force a door God has not opened, to grasp by scheming what he has promised to give. Abraham, tired of waiting for the promised son, fathered a child by his own arrangement and reaped years of sorrow. The Bible counsels a different way: “Be still before the Lord and wait patiently for him; fret not yourself” (Psalm 37:7). Stillness and freedom from fretting are the marks of a heart that truly waits.

This quiet trust is not resignation but rest — a deliberate handing over of the outcome to God. “For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him” (Psalm 62:5). When anxiety rises, the answer is not to act frantically but to return to God and rest again in his character. He has never failed those who trust him, and he will not begin with you. The waiting soul can afford to be calm, because the One it waits for is faithful.

Wait expectantly, watching for God to act

Waiting on God is not a dull endurance but a hopeful expectancy. We wait for someone — someone we are sure will come. The prophet models this eager confidence: “But as for me, I will look to the Lord; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me” (Micah 7:7). Notice the certainty — my God will hear me. True waiting keeps watching, keeps expecting, keeps its eyes on the horizon.

And God honours such expectancy. The Psalmist testifies from experience: “I waited patiently for the Lord; he inclined to me and heard my cry. He drew me up from the pit of destruction... and set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm 40:1–2). The waiting was real, and so was the rescue. Those who have trusted God for the impossible and watched him provide will tell you that the answer, when it came, was worth every day of the wait — and that the God met in the waiting was the greatest gift of all.

Keep serving while you wait

Waiting on God is not an excuse to put life on hold. While we wait for one thing, God has plenty of other things for us to be doing faithfully. The servant in Jesus’ parable was told, “Engage in business until I come” (Luke 19:13) — keep working, keep serving, keep being faithful in the ordinary duties, until the Master returns or the answer arrives. Fruitful waiting keeps its hands busy even as its heart hopes.

So do not let a season of waiting become a season of paralysis. Keep loving the people in front of you, keep doing the good you can do today, keep growing in the things God has already made clear. “Let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9). Often the very faithfulness we show while waiting is part of what God is using to prepare us for what comes next. Waiting and working are not opposites; the one who waits well is the one who keeps steadily at the tasks already in hand, trusting that no labour done for the Lord is ever wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Let waiting do its work in you

Some of God’s best gifts are given not at the end of the waiting but during it. Waiting cultivates patience, humility, and a deeper dependence on God that no shortcut could produce. “The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him. It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord” (Lamentations 3:25–26). The waiting itself is called good — not merely the thing waited for.

So do not treat a season of waiting as time to be endured until real life resumes. It is real life, and God is at work in it, shaping you into someone who can hold his gifts without being ruined by them. Many look back on their long waits as the seasons in which they came to know God most intimately, when stripped of every other prop they learned that he alone is enough. What feels like delay is often the very place of your deepest growth.

How to wait well today

Practically, how do we wait on God? Keep bringing the matter to him in prayer, and then leave it with him rather than snatching it back. Steady yourself on his promises, rehearsing his faithfulness when impatience rises. Refuse the shortcuts that would force his hand. And take courage: “Wait for the Lord; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!” (Psalm 27:14) — a command repeated for emphasis, because waiting takes strength and God supplies it.

Whatever you are waiting for — an answered prayer, an open door, a healing, a change that seems never to come — you are not waiting in vain, and you are not waiting alone. The God you wait for is good, wise, and faithful, and he is nearer in the waiting than you know. Renew your strength in him, watch for the morning, and trust that the One who has appointed the time will not be a moment late. Those who wait for the Lord are never, in the end, put to shame. The wait may be long, but the God at the end of it is worth every moment — and the strength he gives to those who wait is a strength the hurried never know.
